title: Behar: proclaim liberty (Leviticus 25:8–10)
hook: in the fiftieth year, "proclaim liberty throughout the land"

segments.voice: Yesterday, shmita: every seventh year the land rests. Your line was the land rests too. Today, what happens after seven of those sevens.

In Philadelphia there's a cracked bell that people line up to see. Around its crown runs an inscription, with a chapter and verse beside it: proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof. It was cast in the 1750s for the Pennsylvania State House. Later, abolitionists adopted it and gave it the name it carries now, the Liberty Bell. The words were already ancient. They come from Leviticus 25, and from a year the Torah calls the yovel.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `THE WORDS AROUND ITS CROWN.` → `LEVITICUS 25.`

segments.voice: Count seven sabbatical years, seven times seven, forty-nine years. Then, on Yom Kippur of the next year, the shofar sounds through the whole land. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land unto all the inhabitants thereof; it shall be a jubilee unto you". Land that was sold goes back to the family that held it. Israelites who sold themselves into service go free, home to their families. Every fifty years, the board resets. Now the words. Yovel is the ram's horn; the Talmud says that in Arabia they called a ram yovla. The year is named for the sound that announces it, and through Latin, yovel became our English jubilee. The word for liberty, deror, Rashi explains as the freedom to live wherever you wish, not under someone else's control. Some link it to a bird, the deror, that nests freely wherever it likes. And honesty about history: the Talmud says the jubilee was kept only while all the tribes lived on their land, and stopped once they were exiled. Whether it was ever fully practiced is debated, and the sources are thin. But the idea outlived the practice: land and people aren't meant to be owned forever, and debts and losses shouldn't pass down without end. A bell in Philadelphia carries the words still.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES SEVEN YEARS.` · `LAND RETURNS, PEOPLE GO HOME.` · `YOVEL: THE RAM'S HORN.` · `KEPT ONLY WHILE THE TRIBES WERE HOME.` · then, large: `PROCLAIM LIBERTY.`

segments.voice: Think of something someone owes you: money, maybe, or an apology you've waited years for, a favor never returned. Ask whether it's time for a jubilee, not because they've earned it, but because fifty years is long enough, or five. Picture deciding, inside, you owe me nothing for this anymore, and notice what changes when the debt is gone.
Yovel. The jubilee: the fiftieth year, announced by the ram's horn, when land returns, people go free, and liberty is proclaimed throughout the land.
Your line: proclaim liberty. The ram's horn sounds for everyone in the land. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The jubilee is not observed today; rabbinic law holds it lapsed when the tribes were exiled. Jews read Behar in synagogue each year, and the jubilee's ideal of release is often cited in Jewish teaching on debt and freedom.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 25:10 quoted from memory; confirm wording, especially 'hallow' and 'jubilee unto you'.

The Liberty Bell inscription follows the KJV ('Proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof'); the hook gives it in lowercase without quotation marks. Cast 1752–53 for the Pennsylvania State House; the name 'Liberty Bell' came from abolitionists in the 1830s. Confirm.
Rosh Hashanah 26a: Rabbi Akiva heard 'yovla' for a ram in Arabia; confirm.
Rashi on 25:10 (from Rosh Hashanah 9b): deror as dwelling wherever one wishes; the bird (dror) link is a traditional explanation. Confirm.
Arakhin 32b: jubilee observed only when all tribes dwell on their land; confirm. Historical practice is debated; the script says so.
Hook softened from 'more than two thousand years old' to 'already ancient', since the dating of Leviticus is debated among scholars.
'Yovel became our English jubilee through Latin' (iubilaeus, influenced by iubilare): confirm.
